question: What is the primary difference between an episiotomy and an obstetric laceration?

options.A: An episiotomy requires suturing but lacerations always heal without intervention.
options.B: Lacerations only occur in the vaginal mucosa whereas episiotomies involve muscle.
options.C: Lacerations are performed by obstetricians while episiotomies are done by midwives.
options.D: An episiotomy is a controlled surgical incision while a laceration is an accidental tear.

explanation: Surgical incisions have clean, predictable margins made with scissors or a blade, whereas tears feature ragged edges caused by mechanical stretching beyond tissue limits. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T011#GNS226_U4_T011_h1)

question: Why is prompt anatomical repair of deep perineal and genital tears necessary?

options.A: To restore normal function and prevent long-term morbidity
options.B: To ensure immediate cessation of lochia rubra flow
options.C: To accelerate the process of normal postpartum uterine involution
options.D: To prevent the development of postpartum pre-eclampsia

explanation: Accurate realignment of torn muscular and fascial planes ensures proper healing, preserves urinary and fecal continence, and avoids chronic pain. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T011#GNS226_U4_T011_h1)

question: What is the primary structural role of the perineal body during childbirth?

options.A: It controls the hormonal triggers that initiate the second stage of labour.
options.B: It forms the rigid bony framework of the lower pelvic outlet.
options.C: It secretes lubricating fluids to ease the passage of the fetal head.
options.D: It acts as a central tendon and anchor point for multiple perineal muscles.

explanation: The perineal body provides structural integrity to the pelvic floor by uniting several muscles of the perineum in a dense fibromuscular node. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T011#GNS226_U4_T011_h2)

question: Which muscle group forms the primary supportive sling of the pelvic floor?
explanation: The levator ani muscles wrap around the vagina, urethra, and rectum to maintain pelvic organ support and maintain continence. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T011#GNS226_U4_T011_h2)

question: A perineal tear that involves the vaginal mucosa and perineal muscles but leaves the anal sphincter intact is classified as what degree?
explanation: Second-degree tears involve the perineal muscles and skin/mucosa but do not extend into the anal sphincter complex. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T011#GNS226_U4_T011_h3)

question: Which classification of perineal trauma involves disruption of the rectal mucosa?
explanation: A fourth-degree tear is the most extensive classification, characterized by injury to the anal sphincters as well as the epithelium of the rectum. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T011#GNS226_U4_T011_h3)

question: Which patient group is statistically at the highest risk for severe perineal lacerations?

options.A: Nulliparous women experiencing a rapid instrumental delivery
options.B: Multiparous women with a history of precipitous deliveries
options.C: Multiparous women delivering a low birth weight infant
options.D: Women undergoing an elective Caesarean section at term

explanation: First-time mothers have tighter, unstretched perineal tissues, and instruments further increase the risk of soft tissue trauma. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T011#GNS226_U4_T011_h4)

question: What is the primary mechanism by which a persistent occipitoposterior position causes perineal tearing?

options.A: It causes premature rupture of membranes and uterine hyperstimulation.
options.B: It directly damages the anal sphincter prior to the onset of crowning.
options.C: It presents a wider fetal head diameter to the pelvic outlet, increasing stretching.
options.D: It prevents the engagement of the fetal head in the pelvic brim.

explanation: An occipitoposterior position forces the fetal head to deflex, presenting a larger circumference that strains the perineal tissues. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T011#GNS226_U4_T011_h4)

question: When should the initial comprehensive inspection of the perineum and vagina take place?

options.A: Twenty-four hours after the completion of the third stage
options.B: Prior to the onset of the second stage of labour
options.C: Immediately after the rupture of fetal membranes
options.D: Immediately following the delivery of the placenta

explanation: Postpartum assessment of the genital tract is routinely performed immediately after placental delivery to identify and repair trauma promptly. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T011#GNS226_U4_T011_h5)

question: A midwife suspects a third-degree perineal tear after a difficult vacuum delivery. What specific assessment step is mandatory to confirm this?

options.A: Administer a local anesthetic block before touching the area
options.B: Catheterize the bladder to check for hematuria and urethral tears
options.C: Measure the depth of the vaginal wall laceration with a sterile ruler
options.D: Perform a digital rectal examination to check anal sphincter tone

explanation: A rectal examination allows the clinician to palpate the sphincter muscles and assess if the internal or external sphincters are disrupted. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T011#GNS226_U4_T011_h5)

question: Which type of suture material is standard for repairing perineal lacerations?
explanation: Synthetic absorbable materials provide adequate tensile strength during initial healing and break down naturally without requiring removal. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T011#GNS226_U4_T011_h6)

question: When repairing a vaginal and perineal laceration, where should suturing typically begin?

options.B: At the apex of the vaginal tear
options.D: At the midpoint of the perineal skin

explanation: Starting at the apex of the vaginal component allows the clinician to locate the highest point of the wound and secure hemostasis before closing inferiorly. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T011#GNS226_U4_T011_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of applying a cold pack to the perineum in the first twenty-four hours post-repair?

options.A: To stimulate rapid closure of the vaginal apex
options.C: To prevent the development of lochia rubra
options.D: To minimize local edema and reduce pain

explanation: Cold therapy induces vasoconstriction, which decreases swelling and numbs nerve endings to provide immediate pain relief. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T011#GNS226_U4_T011_h7)

question: Why is dietary management involving high-fiber foods emphasized following a deep perineal repair?

options.A: To prevent constipation and avoid straining on the sutures
options.B: To stimulate increased production of breast milk for the infant
options.C: To accelerate the natural absorption of synthetic suture material
options.D: To prevent postpartum anemia by improving iron absorption

explanation: Soft stools reduce the physical pressure and mechanical strain placed on the newly repaired perineal muscles and anal sphincter complex during defecation. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T011#GNS226_U4_T011_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a recognized short-term complication of poor perineal repair? (Select the negative frame)

options.A: Pelvic organ prolapse caused by decade-long muscle atrophy
options.B: Wound dehiscence and localized infection of the sutures
options.C: Local wound hematoma formation within the soft tissues
options.D: Excessive postpartum hemorrhage from bleeding vessels

explanation: Pelvic organ prolapse is a long-term consequence of support failure, whereas hemorrhage, hematoma, and dehiscence occur immediately in the postpartum period. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T011#GNS226_U4_T011_h8)

question: What is a common long-term consequence for women with an unrecognized third- or fourth-degree perineal tear?
explanation: Disruption of the anal sphincter complex that goes unrepaired permanently impairs bowel control, leading to involuntary loss of gas or stool. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T011#GNS226_U4_T011_h8)
